name: Kensington Runestone
hook: A Minnesota farm find of 1898, runically dated 1362, that two professors judged not medieval in 1899.
claim: Olof Öhman reported finding a rune-inscribed stone on his farm near Kensington, Minnesota, in 1898. Its text, dated 1362, tells of 30 Norwegians and Swedes out of Vinland who lost ten men, read by proponents as proof of Norse explorers deep inland.

claimed_age.label: AD 1362 (date carved in the text)
claimed_age.basis: The date written in the inscription itself; no independent dating method applies.

accepted_age.label: 19th century AD, before 1898; carver unknown
accepted_age.basis: Weight of linguistic and runic evidence (Williams 2012). No physical method dates the carving; 150 BP (AD 1800) marks the start of the 19th century, not a measured limit.

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: Norse voyages to Vinland were known only from sagas and annals, the last recorded long before 1362; nothing placed Norse explorers in the interior.

unambiguous_signal.note: Clearly a deliberate carving; the dispute was over its age and author, not whether people made it.

documented_context.note: No corroborating witness or tangible evidence fixes where or how it was found; only the finders' statements exist.

multiple_dating_methods.note: No dating method was applied; its age rested on the carved date and on readings of its runes and language.

multiple_labs.note: No laboratory work. The only 1899 examinations were Breda's reading of a drawing and Curme's inspection in Chicago.

professional_recovery.note: The farmer found it partly under a young tree whose roots gripped it; no trained excavator saw it in place.

peer_reviewed_report.note: No report by ~1903: after the 1899 verdicts the stone 'was not therefore submitted to a detailed examination' and became a door-step.

material_accessible.note: Öhman let it go to Chicago for inspection in 1899; it then lay at his granary as a door-step. No refusal of access is recorded.

independent_teams.note: Breda (Minneapolis) and Curme (Chicago) assessed it separately in 1899 and both rejected a medieval date; no second group backed the claim.

proponent_stake.note: No stake is documented for 1898-1903. Holand's financial interest (a purchase, or a share per Flom) began in 1907.

objections.text: Thirty explorers could not plausibly have reached western Minnesota from Vinland on the Atlantic coast, and covering that distance in fourteen days would have been impossible.
objections.raised_by: Skeptics, as summarized by George T. Flom
objections.outcome_note: No trace of a Norse inland route has been found, but Williams (2012) says 'nothing has been proven either way'; the medieval claim fell on the text, not the route.

objections.text: Plural subjects take singular verb forms (vi var, vi kom), where 14th-century Swedish had -um endings (vi varom, vi komom); the text reads as a modern dialect.
objections.outcome_note: Williams (2012): the weight of evidence still favors a 19th-century origin, though several forms once called impossible proved possible in Old Swedish.

objections.text: The text is written 'in modern runic characters'; runes were used in Dalarna long after the Middle Ages, so a 19th-century carver could have known them.
objections.outcome_note: Rune-rows of 1883 and 1885 from Dalarna (Larsson papers, found 2004) are closely related to the stone's runes, though n, o, p, r and t differ (Williams 2012).

objections.text: Runes cut in the soft calcite part are as clear as those in the harder graywacke; long weathering would have blurred them.
objections.outcome_note: Winchell (MHS 1910) judged the weathering old, as Wolter's books (2006, 2009) do; none of this is peer-reviewed or replicated (Williams 2012).

objections.text: No independent witness saw the stone in place, and accounts of the enclosing tree's size and age varied from one telling to the next.
objections.outcome_note: Williams (2012): no corroborating witness or tangible evidence exists, but there is also 'no evidence to disprove the account'.

objections.text: The inscription's number system and historical setting do not fit the 14th century, so the stone is not authentic.
objections.outcome_note: Flom (1910) judged Gjessing's case sound; no later source read for this record re-tests the numerals.

objections.text: Öhman owned a grammar with a runic alphabet, given him by a defrocked minister, Fogelblad, pointing to a local maker.
objections.outcome_note: Williams (2012) finds three medieval-looking words of the text in Rosander's Swedish encyclopedia, which Öhman owned, yet no evidence that he carved it; a reported confession fails scrutiny.

status_note: Specialists have judged the text not medieval since 1899, despite a conditional 1910 MHS endorsement. Williams (2012) agrees on the weight of evidence but calls the 19th-century case incomplete; weathering claims of age lack peer review.
what_settled_it: The text itself: Breda and Curme (1899) and later specialists judged its language and runes not medieval. In 2004, rune-rows from Dalarna dated 1883 and 1885 turned up that are closely related to its runes, though n, o, p, r and t differ (Williams 2012).

timeline.event: Olof Öhman reports finding the stone on his farm, partly under a young tree whose roots gripped it; his son Edward, aged ten, is present.
O. J. Breda (Minneapolis, from a drawing) and G. O. Curme (Chicago) both judge the inscription not medieval; the stone returns to Öhman.
Öhman sells the stone (or, per Flom, a share in it) to Hjalmar Holand, who writes about it from 1908 until his death in 1963.
MHS Museum Committee gives a favorable opinion (21 Apr), if a Scandinavian specialist agrees; member-geologist N. H. Winchell presents much of its report.
George T. Flom tells the Illinois State Historical Society the text is a modern dialect in modern runes, building on Helge Gjessing's critique.
Erik Wahlgren publishes The Kensington Stone: A Mystery Solved, a book-length rejection of a medieval origin.
Theodore C. Blegen publishes The Kensington Rune Stone: New Light on an Old Riddle, which Williams (2012) groups with Wahlgren's critique.
Linguist Robert A. Hall Jr. publishes The Kensington Rune-Stone: Authentic and Important, defending a 14th-century origin.
Rune-rows dated 1883 (Carl Emil Larsson) and 1885 (his brother Edward, a Dalarna tailor) are found in the Umeå dialect archive.
Richard Nielsen and geologist Scott F. Wolter publish The Kensington Rune Stone: Compelling New Evidence, a book-length case for authenticity.
Henrik Williams (Uppsala) finds the weight of evidence favors a 19th-century origin but calls that case 'not complete'.
David M. Krueger's Myths of the Rune Stone traces how faith in the stone shaped local Nordic identity after experts undermined it.

falsifier: Overturned by a peer-reviewed, replicated weathering study showing the grooves need centuries of exposure, by 14th-century examples of the stone's rune and verb forms, or by securely dated medieval Norse material from the find area.

confidence_note: S1, S9 and S12 were read for every passage used. Wahlgren, Blegen, Hagen, Hall and the Wolter books were not read; their stances come from titles and S9.
corrections: A reported deathbed confession by a neighbour who claimed to have helped Öhman 'does not stand up to scrutiny' (Williams 2012, S9); no evidence shows Öhman carved the stone.
Crossref's chapter record (10.5749/9781452945422-005) dates Krueger's Myths of the Rune Stone to 2010; the book is 2015 (10.5749/9781452974729).
notes: Carver and motive are unknown: Williams (2012) finds no evidence Öhman made it, so 'hoax' is the best-fitting code, and a 19th-century carving made without intent to deceive is not ruled out. Wolter's geological case (S13, S14) continues Winchell's 1910 view that the weathering is old; it is in books, not peer-reviewed journals, and its data (e.g. mica weathering in the grooves) are UNVERIFIED here. Thalbitzer (1951) also backed authenticity (S9). Hagen's 1950 Speculum study (S2) was not read. 'stratigraphy' here means only the tree-root testimony. The MHS report records hearsay (Gunder Johnson) that Öhman drew runes on a board around 1883.

plates.caption: The Kensington Runestone, showing the runes carved on its face.

open_issues: Winchell did not chair the MHS committee: its 1910 report names E. C. Mitchell as chairman. Winchell was the member-geologist who judged the weathering old and read much of the report (S12, S9); the record says so.

year_resolved set to 1899, when Breda and Curme rejected the stone; specialists never reversed. The MHS 1910 opinion was conditional, and Williams puts the broad academic verdict around 1950; status_note flags the 1910 endorsement.

Kept 'stratigraphy' as the nearest schema term for the tree-root find-context argument; it rests on testimony only (S9), as documented_context = no records. independent_methods_count = 3: text, find context, weathering.

Sköld (2003), DAUM-Katta 13, not added: its host was unreachable, so it is known only from Williams fn 36. Williams dates the Larsson find to 2004 yet cites this 2003 issue; the record follows Williams.
Hagen (1950, S2) dropped from key_proponents and the timeline: his stance could not be confirmed (paywalled) and Williams does not list him. Öhman dropped as finder, not advocate, to fit six names.
The find-context and numerals objections are coded 'unresolved', not 'held': Williams says the find account was never proven false, and no source read re-tests the numerals.
